description.narrative: Stöd till regeringen i Mocambique via UN Joint Program (implementerat av UNICEF och ILO) för att förbättra täckningen och kvalitet av det nationella sociala trygghetssystemet. Programmet som nu går in I sin andra fas fokuserar på att stärka den institutionella kapaciteten på den genomförande myndigheten INAS och på ansvarigt ministerium, ministeriet för jämställdhet, barn och social trygghet (MGCAS). Sverige kommer att i dialog med regeringen (främst via ovan nämnda institutioner) arbeta för ökad täckning av mottagare av regelbundet utbetalda kontantstöd samt för en ökning av beloppen som betalas ut.

Support to the Government of Mozambique via the UN Joint Programme (implemented by UNICEF and ILO) to increase the coverage and quality of the social protection system. The program, commencing its second phase, will focus on strenghtening the institutional capacity at the implementing national agency INAS and at the responsible ministry, Ministry for Gender, Children and Social Action, MGCAS. Sweden will in its dialogue with the government (mainly with the above mentions national structures) work for an increased coverage of beneficiaries for regularly paid social cash transfers as well as an increase of the cash transfers' amounts.

description.narrative:
Outcome 1. Child Grant (02 years) consolidated and expanded
Under Outcome 1, the UNJPSP supported continued expansion and consolidation of the Child Grant (02 years) component of the Basic Social Subsidy Programme (PSSB). By the end of 2025, the programme had reached a cumulative total of 61,725 children covered by the CG, achieving 100 per cent of the UNJPSP target. Additional financial contributions mobilized through the programme enabled the expansion of the Child Grant beyond its original caseload and geographic scope, supporting the inclusion of additional 13,000 beneficiaries in Niassa Province and new districts in Nampula and Cabo Delgado Provinces. This investment enabled more vulnerable children and caregivers to access social protection services while further strengthening the Government's capacity to scale up and deliver social assistance at scale. The expansion was accompanied by sustained investments in frontline capacity, case management, and service delivery systems. Importantly, these investments were intentionally designed as system-strengthening measures, enhancing the delivery of social assistance beyond the Child Grant and generating benefits across a broader range of social protection programmes and services.
A comprehensive package of capacity building reached more than 450 social workers and communitylevel actors, strengthening national systems for case management, referral, monitoring and followup. The scaleup of case management enabled targeted support to the most vulnerable households, including adolescent caregivers and children facing protection risks, while reinforcing coordination between social protection, health, civil registration and protection services. By the end of the year, tens of thousands of children and caregivers had been reached through structured case management, with clear gains in service quality, accountability and followup.
The programme also marked a significant milestone in advancing adaptive and shockresponsive social protection. Through an Anticipatory Action intervention to drought in Magude district, 4,850 households received early cash support linked to forecastbased triggers, demonstrating for the first time the operational feasibility of anticipatory cash transfers within national systems. This experience generated critical lessons to inform future scaleup and contributed to national dialogue on shockresponsive social protection.
Outcome 2. Information management, monitoring and delivery systems strengthened
Under Outcome 2, the UNJPSP made sustained investments in core delivery systems, including digitalization, payment systems, monitoring and grievance redress mechanisms. Progress in rolling out digital payments was uneven, reflecting structural constraints such as mobile network coverage, liquidity challenges and insecurity in some districts. Nevertheless, more than 8,700 beneficiaries received transfers via mobile money in 2025, and foundational work was completed to enable further scaleup in 2026. To strengthen programme monitoring and accountability, the programme also piloted a Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM) system, enabling direct beneficiary feedback on payment receipt and related implementation issues. Complementary improvements to the Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM), including the piloting of a mobile GRM application and preparatory work on a USSDbased platform, strengthened accountability, transparency and accessibilityparticularly for beneficiaries without smartphones. In addition, advantage was taken of the INAS Capacity Assessment exercise to carry out the Spot Checks in eight additional delegations. A total of approximately 576 beneficiaries were consulted, with 72 randomly selected beneficiaries surveyed and interviewed in each delegation.
Significant investments were also made in institutional capacity at decentralized level, through capacity building, the provision of vehicles, ICT equipment, and operational kits for INAS delegations and community workers. These inputs proved critical for maintaining service delivery in fragile and hardtoreach contexts and for supporting programme expansion without compromising quality. Besides, as part of the projects capacity-building component, the UNJP contributed to the revision of the TRANSFORM Shock-Responsive Social Protection module (lead in the MENA region), helping develop updated training materials that are expected to be piloted and adapted in Mozambique as part of the forthcoming African rollout.
Outcome 3. Social protection evidence base and policy strengthened
Under Outcome 3, the UNJPSP strengthened the evidence base and policy framework for social protection reform. Key achievements included completion of the Social Protection Systems Readiness Assessment, which assessed institutional, operational and political preparedness for shock response and directly informed the ongoing development of ENSSB III and revisions to the PASDPE operational framework. The programme also supported the launch of PostDistribution Monitoring (PDM) as a core accountability and learning mechanism for the Child Grant, establishing a structured, governmentowned monitoring cycle to inform continuous programme improvement. Further, A TRANSFORM training on ShockResponsive Social Protection was delivered to journalists ten media, including radio and television) from nine provinces, members of parliament (from three political parties) and Civil Society representatives, helping to build a more informed constituency capable of shaping public debate, policy attention and accountability on adaptive social protection.
The programme also supported an independent monitoring exercise of the PAUS programme, generating practical evidence and recommendations for INAS and DNAS to inform the revision of the programme manual. The exercise covered 8 social units and services reaching at least 497 registered beneficiaries. The INAS Capacity Assessment was finally conducted throughout the 31 INAS delegations and additionally to the social units.
Complementary analytical work on social protection financing, including budget analysis, fiscal and social modelling (MOZMOD), and highlevel policy dialogue, strengthened advocacy efforts at a time of severe fiscal pressure.
This progress was underpinned by of a joint UN approach and strong positioning of both UNICEF and ILO within the national social protection sector, combining trusted government partnerships and sustained engagement with other development partners, solid implementation track records, and coordinated evidence based advocacy to influence policy level reforms while remaining closely anchored in decentralized delivery contexts.
